segments.narration: A star dropped twenty-two percent of its light. Then brightened. Then dipped again, on no schedule at all.
Volunteers sifting Kepler telescope data flagged it in 2015. About fifteen hundred light years away, in Cygnus.

A planet blocks maybe one percent. This was twenty-two. Something enormous and ragged was crossing the star, and nobody could name it. So astronomers said the quiet part out loud: alien megastructure.
The test was colour. A solid object blocks every wavelength equally. Dust does not.
The star dimmed more in ultraviolet than in infrared. Whatever crosses it is fine dust, not a swarm of panels. The most famous alien signal of the decade turned out to be a cloud of grit.

verdicts.claim: KIC 8462852 showed irregular, aperiodic brightness drops reaching up to about 22 percent.

verdicts.claim: Planet Hunters volunteers found the dips in Kepler data and the findings were published in a 2015 paper led by Tabetha Boyajian; the star lies about 1,470 light-years away in Cygnus.
verdicts.note: 79% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Astronomer Jason Wright and others raised a Dyson swarm or similar artificial structure as a speculative explanation for the dimming.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia names Jason T. Wright and others speculating about a Dyson swarm, and notes it was always flagged as highly speculative — which the narration mirrors by calling it 'the quiet part'.

verdicts.claim: An opaque solid object would block all wavelengths of light equally, so wavelength-dependent dimming rules one out.
verdicts.note: Space.com quotes lead author Huan Meng on exactly this reasoning: an object bigger than a dust grain would dim all wavelengths uniformly.

verdicts.claim: A January 2018 study led by Boyajian found the star dims more in ultraviolet than in infrared, indicating fine dust rather than a solid object.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia dates the study to January 2018 and quotes the finding that the blocking material filters wavelengths differently so it cannot be an opaque object; Space.com reports the UV-versus-infrared result and the dust conclusion.
